current_episode.title: Episode 78: Featuring George Cacoulidis, CEO, Grand Metro Properties

guest.bio_context: George Cacoulidis is the second-generation CEO of Grand Metro Properties, which was founded by his father John in 1985. He grew up in the family business before leaving to build a 20-year corporate transactional law practice, during which he represented clients in motorsports and other industries. He returned to Grand Metro as COO in 2015 and has since assumed full leadership, expanding the portfolio across Maine and New York.

context.transcript_excerpt: I'd like to welcome our listeners to the Bolas Beat Podcast. I'm your host, Greg Bolas. Bolas Company is Northern New England's largest commercial real estate services firm with offices in Portland, Maine, as well as Manchester and Portsmouth, New Hampshire. We've been selling and leasing real estate in Maine and New Hampshire since 1975. This podcast is designed to provide insight into Maine's real estate movers and shakers. And speaking of real estate, I'd like to welcome George Kakulides, CEO of Grand Metro Properties, a real estate investment company, to the bowl of speed. George is the second-generation CEO of Grand Metro Properties, which was founded by his father, John, in 1985. Over the decades, the company has built and operated a portfolio of commercial properties in New York and more recently in Portland, Maine. Having grown up in the business and built a successful career in the legal and corporate side of commercial real estate, George assumed leadership of Grand Metro in 2015. Since then, he has continued expanding the portfolio across Maine and New York while guiding the firm to its next chapter. George, great to have you with us today on the Bull of Speed. Thank you for having me. George, you started your career at Grand Metro Builders, left there to build a 20-year corporate transactional law practice, and then came back as COO. What drew you back to the family business, and how has your legal background shaped the way you approach real estate? That is an interesting question, and one I will try to answer. when i grew up in the business uh i was uh heavily involved in all aspects of the business and my father was a hands-on developer so he threw me into everything uh he was a builder too right He was a builder. He enjoyed building quite a bit. That was his passion. He liked to build things. And he also was a very strict disciplinarian and ran a tight ship, tight-fisted control. He and I, at one point, as I got older, just were bumping heads quite a bit. I had a view of how things should be done. He had a view. I respected my father's view tremendously. I just saw things that I would have liked to have performed differently. He didn't see it that way. and so I felt it was time for me to leave and try something new. I was concerned that everything was, as it should have been at the time, going through my father for all of his decisions, but it was leaving me to the side and affecting my growth, my knowledge base, my experience. So I left and I started a legal career. And what I had done, I had noticed when I broke out as a solo attorney that this is the early 90s. All of the legal work that I found in real estate that was exciting and stimulating to me was going away and was going in-house. If you could imagine, in the 1990s, a big real estate development firm, if they paid an in-house attorney $125,000 a year, they were looking at $100 an hour. So the math made sense for them to bring people in, and as they brought people in, I couldn't compete with that. And having a need and a desire to stimulate my mind and not just work on rote projects, I had been involved with motorcycles and bicycles all my life, passions of mine. Motocross? Motocross. and I raced and I wrote a letter to a magazine, I believe it was called Road Racing World, a gentleman who owns it named John Ulrich. Never had the chance to meet him in person and thank him. Unbeknownst to me, I had written a letter to him seeking his personal advice. How do I get involved in racing? It was a passion of mine. Please let me know. What do you suggest I do? Unbeknownst to me, he printed my letter in a letter to the editor and I got two phone calls. One was from a gentleman named Steve DeCamp, who owned the Hooter Suzuki motorcycle racing team. and another from Bob McClain who owned Red Bull Yamaha, the top American team in Grand Prix racing in motorcycling, which is now MotoGP. pending_qa.q: How can a legal background in corporate transactions inform commercial real estate investment strategy?
pending_qa.r: Cacoulidis' legal experience, particularly his work assembling teams in motorsports and other industries with clients like Don Painos, taught him how to develop cohesive teams and navigate complex corporate environments across multiple industries. This skill set enabled him to return to the family business with the ability to manage stakeholders, negotiate effectively, and make decisions quickly—translating corporate discipline into real estate operations.

pending_qa.q: What role did a magazine letter about motorsports play in shaping a real estate executive's career trajectory?
pending_qa.r: In the early 1990s, Cacoulidis wrote a letter to Road Racing World magazine seeking advice on entering motorsports. The editor John Ulrich printed the letter, resulting in calls from Steve DeCamp of Hooter Suzuki and Bob McClain of Red Bull Yamaha. This led him to work with Don Painos, who founded Mylan Laboratory and owned racing operations, providing mentorship and exposure to corporate operations across multiple industries before he returned to real estate.

pending_qa.q: Why did a historic 1970s Yankee Stadium renovation project require burying equipment in the outfield?
pending_qa.r: George's father, who renovated the old Yankee Stadium in the 1970s during Mayor Beam's administration, needed to show rapid progress to justify continued political support for the costly project. He laid sod across the infield to make the stadium appear nearly complete when the Mayor visited, then buried equipment in the outfield because complex union rules and competing contractors created delays; subcontractors could not retrieve their equipment quickly due to strict labor agreements limiting work by specific trades.

pending_qa.q: What was the visionary but controversial proposal for a 60-acre former Irving Oil property in South Portland?
pending_qa.r: In the early 1990s, George's father purchased 60 acres of land formerly owned by Al Glickman (known as Bug Light) and envisioned building two or three 30-foot-tall buildings connected by cable car to Fourth Street in the Old Port or Eastern Promenade. George describes his father as having a go-big-or-go-home ethos and a vision for a convention center, but the proposal brought New York-scale ambition to a South Portland market that was not ready for it, and no convention center was ultimately built.

pending_qa.q: How did acquiring Hope Island in Casco Bay represent a family's first entry into Maine real estate investment?
pending_qa.r: George's parents purchased Hope Island in Casco Bay as their first Maine property because his mother wanted to return to her roots growing up on a farm, and his father found a compelling deal: 88 acres for $1.3 million. His father beat out competing buyers by accepting the property as-is without demanding concessions, leveraging his builder background to see development potential. This purchase led to more frequent visits to Portland and eventually to the acquisition of the Bug Light property.

pending_qa.q: What competitive bidding situation in 2017 led to acquiring a South Portland office property with a major leaseback arrangement?
pending_qa.r: In 2017, George purchased 82 Running Hill Road in South Portland, an office building originally built by his brother and then occupied by Fairchild, in a competitive bidding situation against several interested parties. He bought it from Dead River Company and secured a 13-year leaseback, creating a sale-leaseback structure. The timing was favorable as South Portland and Portland were experiencing business growth, though the investment would be tested three years later by COVID.

pending_qa.q: How does the principle of avoiding emotional attachment influence real estate portfolio management?
pending_qa.r: George's father advised him: do not fall in love with the building, fall in love with the money—focus on cash flow and asset performance. Applying this principle, George divested from two emotionally significant Long Island properties, 591 and 595 Stewart Avenue, where he had grown up and worked extensively, because they were underperforming and could not overcome issues from being retaken after the 2008 financial crisis when seller-financed buyers defaulted.

pending_qa.q: What Long Island industrial property sale did a real estate investor regret missing, and how did it influence subsequent decisions?
pending_qa.r: George missed an opportunity to purchase a 250,000-square-foot warehouse on Long Island near exit 60 of the Long Island Expressway in Suffolk County when sellers raised the price from $27 million to $31 million. After he passed, industrial values doubled and the property was eventually leased to a pharmaceutical company. Missing this deal prompted him to pursue other acquisitions within the following five years that deviated from his core philosophy and underperformed, illustrating how a missed opportunity can lead to compensatory poor decisions.

pending_qa.q: What structural impact did COVID-19 have on a Maine-based office portfolio and how did operators adapt?
pending_qa.r: COVID required Grand Metro to reinvest over $10 million in one building to survive, and the post-pandemic period brought significant tenant downsizing, including a major 70,000-square-foot tenant departure. One specific case involved Marshawn Eyewear Company, which was bought by private equity, acquired a 1,000-location Canadian retail company, and relocated its executive team from a high-end corporate office to a warehouse. George embraced hybrid work as a permanent reality and recognized that while office is evolving, tenants and office ownership remain viable if operators adapt.

pending_qa.q: What challenges do office property operators face in the post-pandemic commercial real estate market?
pending_qa.r: George identifies continuous compression of profits and expanding operating expenses as core challenges in office properties, driven by tenant evolution and brokers bringing unrealistic demands or pressure to reduce landlord terms. He notes that aggressive lease negotiations with tenants attempting to 'beat up the landlord' do not result in quality deals or properties that attract or retain tenants, forcing him to reanalyze his office strategy despite his historical preference for that asset class.
